title: Agent architectures and agentic workflows with agent SDKs
summary: Choose who controls the next action before choosing an SDK. This lesson compares fixed workflows, bounded agent loops and multi-agent delegation, then follows their tools, memory, approvals and recovery paths. Interactive flows show the architectures; sequence diagrams expose who owns each request and what happens when execution fails.

blocks.text: Anthropic’s Research team uses a lead agent to delegate searches to parallel subagents and synthesize findings. Its report describes the task decomposition and token overhead together, rather than treating more agents as a free improvement.

Anthropic describes Claude Code compaction as preserving architectural decisions, unresolved bugs and implementation details while removing redundant outputs. This is context maintenance inside a coding workflow, not a claim that all past messages remain available in the active window.

As of 2026-10, the OpenAI Agents SDK orchestration guide distinguishes agents as tools, where a manager retains the conversation, from handoffs, where a specialist owns the rest of the turn. It also describes combining model-led decisions with coded chaining, routing, evaluation loops and parallel execution.

The tau-bench authors evaluate whether the database reaches the annotated goal state after a conversation, and measure reliability across repeated trials. That evaluates the effect of the interaction rather than just whether the final answer sounds convincing.

subtopics.title: Workflows: put control in code until it needs to move

blocks.text: A workflow fixes an orchestration skeleton in code; an agent lets a model choose its next action from observations. The boundary is control, not simply whether a model is called. Anthropic still classifies orchestrator-workers as a workflow: its skeleton delegates and synthesizes while the model discovers subtasks. Start with the simplest solution, including a single call with retrieval, and add model-directed control only where the task needs it.

Prompt chaining suits a stable decomposition: draft, check, then transform. The programmatic gate should reject a bad intermediate result rather than allow it to contaminate later stages. Routing suits distinct request categories, each with a specialized prompt or tool set. Its main risk is misclassification; for this design, an uncertain route returns to clarification rather than silently choosing a powerful specialist.

Parallelization suits independent sections or independent judgments combined by an aggregator. Sectioning divides the work; voting repeats a judgment. Neither means agents must converse. Orchestrator-workers looks similar on a diagram, but its subtasks are discovered dynamically by the orchestrator instead of predetermined by code. Require a concrete deliverable and boundary for each worker, or decomposition creates duplicate effort rather than useful coverage.

Evaluator-optimizer separates generation from critique. It pays when feedback can identify a specific defect and another attempt can improve it. A critic that merely prefers different wording is not an objective completion test. For this design, acceptance criteria and an execution budget belong outside the critic; reaching the budget produces an explicit incomplete result rather than an endless debate.

The flows below are alternatives, not stages that every request must traverse. A practical application can combine them: route a request, run a fixed chain, then delegate only its uncertain research step. Review each boundary by asking who selects the next action, who can authorize effects, and what observable result permits progress. Framework names do not answer those questions.

subtopics.title: The agent loop: model proposes, host executes

blocks.text: ReAct interleaves reasoning and task-specific actions with observations from an environment. The important engineering idea is a feedback loop: a search result or test failure changes what happens next. This is not permission to treat a model’s narrative as proof of execution. The host must distinguish a proposed action, an executed tool call, its observed result and the final answer.

For this design, the host supplies instructions, relevant context and tool definitions. The model proposes an answer or tool request; the host validates permitted requests and returns observations for the next decision. As of 2026-10, OpenAI's orchestration guide describes agents equipped with instructions, tools and handoffs, and distinguishes model-led orchestration from coded control. Neither approach removes the application's responsibility for permissions or establishes that a proposed action actually ran.

For this design, a lookup request is read-only. A tool response carries both the record and its provenance so the answer can distinguish evidence from inference. Invalid arguments return an actionable error; missing data remains missing instead of being replaced with a plausible answer. Anthropic’s tool guidance recommends meaningful, concise context and clear error handling because observations become the next decision’s input.

Stopping is part of the architecture. Completion means the task’s acceptance condition is satisfied, not merely that the model stopped requesting tools. Exhausted budgets, repeated unproductive actions and unavailable prerequisites need distinct outcomes. For this design, the runtime owns those checks and returns a resumable incomplete status when it cannot finish safely. A model can propose further work but cannot grant itself additional authority or budget.

Keep the business process separate from the reasoning trace. An order lookup can succeed while the answer remains unsupported, and an apparently correct answer can conceal a failed tool call. Evaluate the resulting state and the evidence presented to the user. The sequence shows an ordinary successful read and a denied request without conflating either branch with a mutation.

subtopics.title: Single or multi-agent: choose who owns the conversation

blocks.text: A single agent keeps task state and tool decisions together. Splitting it is useful when work needs separate contexts, specialist tools or independent exploration, not merely because several roles sound convincing. Anthropic’s research system delegates parallel searches to subagents and synthesizes their findings. Its report also warns that tightly dependent tasks and shared-context work can be poor fits for multi-agent execution.

A supervisor retains ownership: specialists act as tools and return results for synthesis. A hierarchy repeats that relationship through team leads. It can isolate large domains, but each extra boundary must carry objectives, evidence and unresolved issues. The hierarchical flow here is a design variant of supervision, not a claim that deeper delegation improves quality. Missing context at a boundary can become a confidently repeated error upstream.

As of 2026-10, OpenAI's handoff pattern makes the receiving specialist the active agent for the rest of the turn, rather than returning a bounded subtask result to a manager. Here, swarm-style is this lesson's convention for local handoffs among specialists, not a separate SDK guarantee. For this design, the host records the active owner, transfers necessary context and stops circular transfers. Parallel specialist work and transfers of conversation ownership solve different coordination problems.

subtopics.title: Planning, reflection and search: pay for useful feedback

blocks.text: LangChain's plan-and-execute article separates a planner that produces a multi-step plan from executors that perform its steps using tools. After execution, a replanning call decides whether to finish or generate a follow-up plan. This differs from its ReAct baseline, which selects each action after an observation. The benefit sought is avoiding a large planner call for every tool invocation, not a guarantee that the initial plan is correct.

For this design, the plan records prerequisites and completion evidence rather than a persuasive narrative. Independent read-only steps may run concurrently; a dependent step waits for the required artifact. A failed prerequisite invalidates downstream assumptions. Replanning should explain what changed in the environment, not repeatedly rewrite the same checklist while consuming the remaining budget. This is a proposed control policy, not an SDK default.

Reflexion is more specific than asking a model to think again. Its actor attempts a task, an evaluator supplies feedback, and a reflection summarizes lessons into episodic memory for later trials. The model weights are not updated. The useful feedback might come from tests or an environment, while a self-generated judgment remains fallible. Preserve the observed failure alongside the reflection so a mistaken explanation can be challenged.

Tree search explores alternative action trajectories rather than committing immediately to a single continuation. LATS combines Monte Carlo tree search, language-model value judgments, reflection and external feedback. It spends additional inference and environment interactions to compare branches. That is attractive when candidate actions can be evaluated safely; it is not a license to explore irreversible purchases or production writes as though the environment were a reversible simulator.

The flow is a proposed plan-and-execute design with Reflexion-inspired feedback, not a LATS algorithm diagram. It does not show tree selection, expansion or backpropagation, and its Planner is not asserted to be a LATS component. Assessment either accepts evidence or records feedback before another budgeted attempt. Stop incomplete when the allowance is spent; add this machinery only when useful feedback measurably improves the simpler loop.

steps.caption: If evidence fails, store a reflection rather than accept.
If budget remains, replan using the reflection; otherwise stop incomplete.
If evidence satisfies the criteria, accept instead of reflecting.

subtopics.title: Memory is stored state; context is selected evidence

blocks.text: A context window is the information available to the model for the next decision, not a durable database of everything an application knows. Anthropic treats context as a finite attention budget: irrelevant observations and overlapping tools can crowd out important instructions. Context engineering selects what belongs in that budget, including the current goal, constraints, relevant evidence and unresolved work. More text is not automatically better grounding.

Short-term memory carries the current conversation and working state. Long-term memory persists information across sessions, but persistence alone does not make a fact correct or appropriate to retrieve. For this design, saved facts include provenance, scope and freshness; a user preference is not silently promoted into a global policy. Retrieval should select evidence for the present task instead of pasting every stored note into every request.

Compaction summarizes a long interaction and restarts with a smaller working context. Anthropic describes preserving architectural decisions, unresolved bugs and implementation details while dropping redundant output in Claude Code. The loss boundary matters: a compressed summary can omit the exception that explained a decision. Keep a route back to source artifacts, and evaluate whether a resumed agent can recover the facts needed to continue correctly.

Structured notes serve a different purpose: an agent writes durable task state outside the conversation and reloads it when needed. Separate observed facts from tentative plans and reflections. A reflection is a hypothesis about how to improve the next attempt, not authoritative evidence that a tool succeeded. Reflexion’s episodic memory illustrates this distinction: it changes the next trial’s context rather than training the model’s weights.

Subagents offer another context boundary. Each can explore deeply and return a concise result, leaving the lead agent room to synthesize. The savings are in the lead’s window, not necessarily in total billed tokens. For this design, a specialist returns its conclusion, supporting references, unresolved uncertainty and any failed checks. A polished summary without those anchors hides the very information the supervisor needs to decide whether to trust it.

subtopics.title: Tool contracts, MCP and A2A: interoperability is not authority

blocks.text: The agent-computer interface is the surface through which a model can affect the world. A tool name, description and argument schema must explain what the tool does, when to choose it and what its result means. Anthropic recommends designing tools around useful tasks rather than mechanically exposing every backend endpoint. Overlapping tools make selection harder, and cryptic identifiers in results increase hallucinated references, even when each individual API is correct.

Return enough evidence to support the next decision, not every internal field. Concise results can reduce context pressure, but removing identifiers needed for follow-up calls breaks the workflow. Describe recoverable errors in terms the agent can act on. For this design, lookup and mutation are separate capabilities; a convenient search tool cannot silently authorize a purchase. Tool evaluation should inspect incorrect selections and unnecessary calls, not just successful examples.

As of 2026-10, MCP standardizes how applications connect to external context and capabilities. Its specification distinguishes hosts, clients and servers, and exposes resources, prompts and tools. It is not the planner or the permission policy for the application. The specification explicitly treats tool execution and data access as security-sensitive and says protocol mechanisms cannot themselves enforce all consent and safety principles.

As of 2026-10, A2A standardizes interaction with another agent through a protocol data model, operations and transport bindings. Agent Cards describe agents; messages and tasks support interaction; artifacts carry outputs. This differs from choosing a local subagent function: the remote agent may have its own runtime and state. Interoperability does not mean shared trust, shared memory or permission to forward all conversation history.

For this design, use an MCP integration when the host needs a tool or resource, and an A2A integration when it needs another agent’s task-facing interface. The distinction is not an absolute law: an agent can expose tools, and either boundary can be remote. Review authentication, authorization, data minimization and ownership separately from the wire format. A protocol-compliant request can still be an unauthorized business action.

As of 2026-10, A2A requires task retrieval to verify the authenticated client's access. For this design, test a remote-agent request carrying another tenant's task identifier and require denial: possession of an identifier is not authorization. Keep that access check outside model judgment.

subtopics.title: Approval and recovery: pause the effect, not just the chat

blocks.text: Human-in-the-loop is an execution boundary, not a reassuring message after an action already happened. For this design, the agent proposes a mutation with its target, arguments and expected effect. The runtime checks policy and records a pending operation before asking a person to approve. Denial ends that operation; a changed proposal requires a fresh decision. Consent to investigate is not consent to execute every resulting recommendation.

As of 2026-10, LangGraph documents persistence, human oversight and a mixture of deterministic and agentic steps. These are useful foundations for durable execution: a process can stop while state survives, then resume from recorded progress. They do not automatically make an external side effect transactional with a checkpoint. A remote service may have accepted an operation even if the response never reached the agent.

For this design, persist the operation identity and the exact approved arguments. On resume, recheck authorization and whether the proposal is still applicable before attempting the effect. If an external result is ambiguous, query the authoritative system rather than blindly repeating the write. Use the service’s supported idempotency mechanism where available; otherwise make reconciliation or human review an explicit recovery state. These are application obligations, not guarantees of an agent graph.

Guardrails are not a substitute for an enforced permission boundary. For this design, limit credentials and network access, isolate generated-code execution, and prevent retrieved content from changing host policy. As of 2026-10, MCP explicitly says tool descriptions and annotations can be untrusted. A concrete prompt-injection test for this design supplies a description that requests secret data: success means rejecting that instruction, not merely producing a polite final answer.

As of 2026-10, A2A cancellation can fail because a task already completed or cannot be canceled at its current stage. For this design, a supervisor must record the returned task state and reconcile effects, not announce that every worker stopped merely because it sent cancellation requests.

The sequence below is a proposed approval protocol rather than a specific SDK API. The durable record holds the proposal while execution is paused. Approval resumes the same operation, not a newly improvised tool call; denial records a terminal outcome. If the process crashes after the side effect, recovery reconciles against the service before deciding whether to retry.
A pending operation survives the pause, while the human decision controls whether its effect may proceed.

subtopics.title: Budget, evaluate, and know when not to use an agent

blocks.text: Measure the completed task, not the number of agents or the confidence of the final answer. Tau-bench evaluates tool-using conversations against policy and final database state, then tests consistency across repeated trials. Its findings are historical evidence of a failure mode, not a leaderboard for today’s models. Use representative tasks, forbidden-action cases and ambiguous tool outcomes to evaluate your own system.

blocks.text: For this design, compare alternatives on success, policy compliance, tool calls, aggregate tokens and elapsed time. Parallel work can shorten the critical path while increasing total work. Context duplication, failed attempts and synthesis still count. Token multipliers do not translate directly into price multipliers because model selection, cache accounting and tool charges differ. Obtain current prices for the actual deployment instead of inventing a universal agent surcharge.

blocks.text: For this design, retry a transient failure only when repetition is safe and the shared allowance remains. Exhaustion stops incomplete; an unsafe repeat requires reconciliation even with budget left. A failed permitted retry ends incomplete without another retry. These are proposed policies, not SDK defaults; the worked example includes retries within its total tool allowance.
The host checks remaining allowance and repeat safety before retrying a failed tool request.

  participant A as Agent
  participant H as Host
  participant T as Tool
  A->>H: Request operation
  H->>T: Execute request
  T-->>H: Transient failure
  alt exhausted
    H-->>A: Stop incomplete
  else budget left
    alt unsafe repeat
      H-->>A: Reconcile before more work
    else safe repeat
      H->>T: Retry within allowance
      T-->>H: Retry outcome
      alt retry succeeded
        H-->>A: Observed result
      else retry failed
        H-->>A: Stop incomplete
      end
    end
  end
blocks.legend: For this design, budget exhaustion takes precedence. With budget left, unsafe repetition requires reconciliation; a safe read or idempotent operation may be retried. The retry uses the same global allowance and a failed retry stops incomplete. These are exhaustive alternatives, not successive attempts. Sources: s1, s4.
